questions.topic: Why Exact k-NN Does Not Scale
questions.question: What work does exact vector search perform?
options: It compares the query against every eligible indexed vector
It descends a tree until it reaches one leaf partition
It follows graph shortcuts until the score stops improving
It decodes each compressed vector and keeps the best few

questions.topic: Why Exact k-NN Does Not Scale
questions.question: What does ANN recall@k measure?
options: The share of labeled relevant documents the search returns
The share of the exact top-k neighbours the approximation returns
The share of queries whose results meet the latency budget
The share of indexed vectors the search actually examines

questions.topic: Why Exact k-NN Does Not Scale
questions.question: Why retain an exact-search implementation after deploying ANN?
options: To serve queries whose filters leave too few candidates to approximate
To rebuild the approximate index whenever its graph becomes fragmented
To provide ground-truth neighbours for regression tests
To handle traffic spikes when the approximate index is being retrained

questions.topic: Why Exact k-NN Does Not Scale
questions.question: When can exact search remain the better production choice?
options: When the corpus is large but every vector has been quantized
When recall matters more than latency, whatever the corpus size
When vectors are low-dimensional enough for pruning to be effective
When filtered partitions are small and exact latency meets the objective

questions.topic: Why Exact k-NN Does Not Scale
questions.question: An index has ANN recall@10 of 1.0 but poor relevance recall@10. What is the likely conclusion?
options: The embedding model's exact neighbourhood is poor for this task
The approximate index is silently dropping true neighbours
The candidate cutoff is too small to reach the relevant documents
The relevance labels disagree with the metric the index was built on

questions.topic: Why Exact k-NN Does Not Scale
questions.question: Which benchmark best supports an ANN production decision?
options: Mean latency at the recall setting the vendor recommends by default
Recall, percentile latency, throughput, memory, updates and filters
Index build time and peak memory across several corpus sizes
Recall measured against the exact baseline at several probe settings

questions.topic: IVF: k-Means Partitioning of the Vector Space
questions.question: How does IVF organize vectors?
options: Into a hierarchy of graph layers with decreasing density
Into fixed-size blocks ordered by the document's insertion time
Into posting lists gathered around learned centroids
Into buckets keyed by a locality-sensitive hash of each vector

questions.topic: IVF: k-Means Partitioning of the Vector Space
questions.question: What does increasing `nprobe` normally do?
options: Raises the number of centroids the index trains during the build
Shrinks each posting list so individual scans finish sooner
Increases the compression applied to vectors inside each list
Searches more cells, raising both recall and latency

questions.topic: IVF: k-Means Partitioning of the Vector Space
questions.question: Why can probing only the nearest centroid miss a true neighbor?
options: A near neighbour can lie just across a coarse cell boundary
Centroids are recomputed per query, so assignments shift between runs
The nearest centroid holds the densest list, which is truncated first
Distances to centroids are approximated, so the ranking is unreliable

questions.topic: IVF: k-Means Partitioning of the Vector Space
questions.question: Why should IVF training vectors represent production traffic?
options: They fix the dimensionality that every later vector must match
They determine the centroids, and so how vectors are assigned to lists
They set the compression codebooks used for the stored vectors
They define the metric the index will use when comparing candidates

questions.topic: IVF: k-Means Partitioning of the Vector Space
questions.question: One IVF list grows far larger than the others after domain drift. What response is strongest?
options: Raise nprobe so the oversized list is no longer the only one searched
Split the list in place and assign the halves to two synthetic centroids
Evaluate retraining the centroids on the new data distribution
Cap the list length and evict the vectors furthest from its centroid

questions.topic: IVF: k-Means Partitioning of the Vector Space
questions.question: A strict filter removes nearly all candidates from probed lists. What risk follows?
options: The filter is applied before scoring, so recall becomes unmeasurable
Probing widens automatically until the latency budget is exhausted
Surviving candidates cluster in one cell, biasing the result set
Post-filtering returns too few results unless the search over-fetches

questions.question: What do HNSW upper layers provide?
options: Sparse long-range links that move the search across the space quickly
A cached shortlist of the most frequently retrieved vectors
Compressed representations used before full-precision rescoring
A partition of the corpus so each layer holds a disjoint subset

questions.question: What does `efSearch` control conceptually?
options: How many neighbours each node is permitted to keep in the graph
The breadth of the candidate frontier held during a query
How many layers the search descends before it begins scoring
The number of entry points the traversal starts from per query

questions.question: What is the usual effect of increasing graph connectivity?
options: Lower memory, because fewer layers are needed to stay navigable
Faster builds, since each insertion evaluates fewer candidate edges
Higher memory, with potentially better navigability
Higher recall at fixed memory, because edges replace stored vectors

questions.question: Why can greedy graph search miss the global nearest neighbor?
options: Edges are undirected, so the traversal can revisit nodes indefinitely
The entry point is chosen at random and may sit far from the query
Distances are computed on compressed vectors during traversal
Traversal can settle in a locally good neighbourhood and stop

questions.question: A workload has heavy insertions and deletions. What must the design evaluate?
options: The engine's update, tombstone and rebuild behaviour
Whether the embedding model stays stable as the corpus changes
How quickly the graph's upper layers can be rebuilt from scratch
Whether recall is measured against a baseline that also changes

questions.question: Why can strict metadata filtering degrade HNSW behavior?
options: The filter forces the index to fall back to a linear scan of the graph
Traversal spends its budget walking through disallowed nodes
Filtered nodes are removed, disconnecting the layers above them
The filter changes which metric the graph edges were built against

questions.question: How does product quantization represent a vector?
options: As a single centroid ID drawn from one global codebook
As a sparse set of the dimensions with the largest magnitudes
As codeword IDs for the learned centroids of each subvector
As a low-precision copy with each dimension rounded to one byte

questions.question: What causes PQ approximation error?
options: Subvectors are assumed independent, so their errors cancel out
The codebooks are trained on a sample rather than the full corpus
Distances are computed in a lower-dimensional projected space
Each subvector is replaced by the nearest codeword available

questions.question: What does asymmetric distance computation keep uncompressed?
options: The query vector, which is compared against the codebooks directly
The database vectors, which are decoded before each comparison
The codebooks, which are held at full precision in memory
The shortlist, which is re-encoded only after the first ranking

questions.question: Why combine IVF and PQ?
options: IVF fixes the recall floor while PQ raises the achievable throughput
IVF narrows the search to a few cells while PQ compresses their vectors
IVF handles filtered queries while PQ handles unfiltered ones
IVF trains on the corpus while PQ adapts to the live query stream

questions.question: How can a system recover quality after PQ candidate scoring?
options: Increase the number of subspaces so each codeword covers less error
Re-run the search with a second codebook and merge the two shortlists
Rerank the shortlist using full-precision vectors
Raise nprobe so more compressed candidates enter the shortlist

questions.question: A 768-dimensional float32 vector is encoded with 96 one-byte subspace IDs. What is its raw code size?
options: 3,072 bytes
768 bytes
384 bytes
96 bytes

questions.question: What normally happens when an ANN search explores more candidates?
options: Both recall and latency tend to rise together
Recall rises while latency stays flat until memory is exhausted
Recall rises and latency falls, since fewer restarts are needed
Recall plateaus immediately while latency grows without bound

questions.question: Which HNSW resource grows when more neighbor links are stored?
options: Query latency, because each hop evaluates more distance computations
The index's memory footprint
Build throughput, because more edges are inserted per vector
Recall variance, because traversals diverge more between queries

questions.question: Why can the highest ANN recall setting be a poor operating point?
options: Recall above the exact baseline indicates the benchmark is mis-specified
Very high recall settings disable the index's filtering fast path
Its marginal gain can breach the end-to-end latency budget
Extra candidates are drawn from cells the filter will reject anyway

questions.question: What must a complete memory estimate include beyond raw vectors?
options: The peak memory used while the embedding model is being served
The size of the corpus in its original document form
The working set of the query encoder under peak concurrency
Index structures, metadata, replicas and build overhead

questions.question: ANN recall rises from 0.98 to 0.995 with no relevance gain and doubled p95 latency. What is the strongest choice?
options: Keep the faster setting unless another requirement justifies the cost
Take the higher recall, since the exact neighbours are the ground truth
Split the difference and tune to the midpoint of the two settings
Raise the candidate cutoff instead, which buys recall more cheaply

questions.question: Why benchmark under production concurrency and filters?
options: They determine which metric the index should have been built with
They change contention, over-fetching and tail latency
They shift the corpus distribution the centroids were trained on
They decide whether recall should be measured before or after filtering
